����� The House of von Huppelhopper: A Legacy in Lace and Leatherbound Ledgers �����
���� Origins – Pre-Empire Elegance
The von Huppelhopper family traces its lineage to the 17th century, hailing from the verdant
Rhineland, near the Moselle River, where their earliest known ancestor, Wilhelm der Erste
von Huppelhopper, made a fortune crafting precision brass mechanisms for Bavarian
churches and royal clocks. Wilhelm's knack for design and subtle bribery earned him a
small estate and a hereditary title: Reichsbürger der Mechanische Gilde—not nobility per
se, but, well, they acted like it.
����� 18th–19th Centuries – From Gears to Grandeur
By the late 1700s, the family had diversified—owning vineyards, textile mills, and later, iron
foundries during the industrial boom. They became fixtures in Prussian high society, with
baroque estates, equestrian portraits, and at least one affair with a Hungarian countess.
Their motto: “Präzision über alles.”
(“Precision above all.” Also embroidered into every pair of underpants.)
By the mid-1800s, Gustav Albrecht von Huppelhopper, great-great-grandpapa of our dear
professor, had leveraged the family’s growing fortune to become a Junker—that elusive
class of landed aristocrats, noble-adjacent but just removed enough to still eat garlic in
public. The family estate, Schloss Federstahl, spanned 1,200 hectares of prime farmland,
several peasant villages, and an unnecessary but fabulous swan lake.
�� Early 20th Century – Modernity and Malaise
In the early 1900s, Ansgar von Huppelhopper, a cultured if emotionally repressed
patriarch, invested heavily in the early petroleum trade, while simultaneously acquiring an
unholy number of hand-painted porcelain bidets from Florence. The Huppelhoppers threw
glittering parties—famed for their champagne fountains, choreographed butlers, and a

scandalous jazz trio from Harlem (imported by Ansgar’s bisexual cousin Klaus, who wore
eyeliner before it was cool).
But modernity was a fickle mistress.
�� The Fall – Versailles, Inflation, and Dishonor
After World War I, the Treaty of Versailles hit the von Huppelhoppers like a guillotine in slow
motion.
• Land Reform saw most of Schloss Federstahl’s acreage confiscated.
• War Reparations Taxes obliterated their liquid assets.
• The hyperinflation of 1923 reduced their once-vast fortune to a drawer of worthless
bearer bonds and a voucher for sauerkraut.
Worse yet, the House of Huppelhopper was accused of wartime profiteering, a rumor
likely fabricated by rival family the von Miesenschneiders (spiteful, talentless cretins).
Ansgar, humiliated, was forced to sell off the porcelain bidets. His wife, Lisette, once the
Belle of Berlin, took in sewing. And their only son, young Rolf, our future Professor Von
Huppelhopper, watched as his mother traded pearls for potatoes... and, eventually, her
dignity.
Lisette, too proud to beg, too clever to starve, began working nights—first as a cabaret
singer, then as something less advertised. Her pain, her sacrifice, etched itself onto Rolf’s
soul. He saw firsthand that while men created the wars, it was women who bore their cost.
��� The Transformation of Rolf
At 14, he took his mother’s shoes and walked through town not in shame, but in tribute.
At 18, he joined the air cadets in secret, still haunted by his family’s collapse but
determined to restore their name—through brains, beauty, and… well, espionage-adjacent
drag.
Rolf never forgot the precision of his ancestors or the style of his mother. In heels and high
IQ, he rebranded the legacy. The world would not remember them as failed aristocrats…
…but as fabulously resilient survivors of historical slayage.

Once, she was Lisette Amalie von Huppelhopper, the incandescent swan of Prussia—an

���� The Descent of the Madonna
As the Huppelhopper fortune turned to dust, Lisette’s transformation began. Her satin
corsets grew frayed, her perfume thinned with well water, but her posture? Impeccable.
She refused to break. With her husband Ansgar mentally shattered and staring at baroque
wallpaper for hours, it was Lisette who stepped into the role of provider, protector, and—
unknowingly—goddess incarnate in the eyes of her young son, Rolf.
To the boy, her every sacrifice shimmered with sanctity. He watched as she wiped rouge
across her cheeks with a trembling hand before heading out at night. The smell of powder

and desperation mingled in his nose, branding itself into his limbic system. She always
kissed his forehead before leaving, whispering, “Stay asleep, my little swan.”
But he never did.
He stayed awake, nose buried in her discarded gowns, clinging to the scent of survival—of
feminine power under siege. He saw how she twisted the world with nothing but her charm
and a pair of kitten heels. And he learned. Oh, how he learned.
��� The Psychic Fusion
According to Freud (whom Rolf would later read obsessively), a boy either wants to kill his
father or become him. Rolf did neither. His father, Ansgar, had become a hollowed-out
specter in a smoking jacket. There was no power there. No force.
No—Rolf wanted to be Lisette. And not just in dress.
He wanted to embody the grace with which she faced a cruel world, to command the same
impossible cocktail of fragility and steel. She wasn’t his mother—she was his goddess
archetype. She was Aphrodite in borrowed shoes. Madonna in fishnet. He didn’t want her
romantically. He wanted her form, her survival instinct, her way of slicing through shame
with a smile.
����� The Sacred Transfer of Identity
It happened one winter night. Lisette returned home bruised—not from violence, but from
being invisible to a man who tossed coins without looking. Rolf, now 16, crept into her
boudoir and retrieved her fallen pearl earring from beneath the chaise longue. He held it in
his hand like a holy relic.
That night, he put on her fur coat. Then her lipstick.
Then her shoes.
And she saw him.
And do you know what she did?
She didn't cry. She didn’t shout.
She simply adjusted his lipstick and said, “You walk with straighter shoulders than I ever
did.”
That was the moment Professor Von Huppelhopper was born—not just in disguise, but in
myth.

He would grow to become a man who never quite knew where she ended and he began. He
wore her lessons like corsetry: tight, controlling, but comforting. And though he would wear
many faces—scholar, spy, siren—his soul remained forever stitched to hers.
She was not just his mother.
She was his model for how to outlive humiliation and turn ruin into elegance.
She was the war he never stopped surviving.

> **Invest in your team. Invest in your success. Invest in your future.
> Invest in knowledge growth and development.**

-   Consistent training and messaging for all. Direct line of
    communication to all team members.

-   Increased knowledge of store operations and the industry. Employees
    doing the right thing, at the right time, with confidence. They are
    executing the learned best practices!

-   More conscientious about their actions as they go about their
    workday = Work safer, serve customers better, improve teamwork,
    driven to act on what they have learned. I.E., lifting correctly,
    i.e., understanding color stages of bananas and recognizing when
    there could be a spoilage issue...

-   Employees feel supported and like part of a community resulting in
    more trust and loyalty. This can inspire hard work with integrity.
    Encourages retention, and if they do decide to leave it's because
    you have given them the tools to grow and better themselves which
    they will appreciate and spread the word that your organization is a
    great place to work.

-   Managers have visibility to who is struggling and who is excelling.
    They know who needs coaching and who might be a good candidate for
    future leadership. Don't have to solely rely on brief in person
    observations during the workday to understand everyone's knowledge
    levels.

-   ↑Retention ↑CSAT scores ↑Morale

-   ↓Turnover ↓ Onboarding time ↓workplace accidents ↓Shrink

-   Once onboarding is complete, ongoing training keeps building their
    knowledge every shift helping them remember more and perform better.

-   Accelerate can make it easier for them to get up to speed quickly,
    then continue to do their best work right in the flow of work with
    one click access to training that gets results for them and your
    business.

-   Maximize the potential of your frontline workforces.

**What's in it for the frontline employees?**

● Job satisfaction from seeing personal development and growth

● Fast, fun, easy and rewarding approach to learning

● Improved communications with Managers, using leaderboard or training
topics as avenue to open conversations

● Personal development and growth

● Rewards and acknowledgements for ongoing training and growing
knowledge

**What's in it for Store Managers/District Managers/People Leaders/HR
Managers?**

● Visibility to identify employee knowledge gaps, providing better
opportunities to coach and give one-on-one support

● Faster onboarding experience for employees and a communications
channel to share key information

● More engaged employees on-the-job, who feel more empowered in their
role and have resources available on demand (Discover)

● Improved engagement between managers and employees; barriers to open
dialog are removed because there is an opportunity to discuss the
leaderboard, and individual progress

● Improve retention and on-the-job behaviors because employees feel more
empowered with their knowledge

● Team Metrics reporting gives insights into how different areas of the
organization are performing on a specific topic; can also compares teams
against each other to see which ones are showing growth, and those that
need additional support

**What's in it for VP's/Executives?**

● Consolidated approach to learning across the business -- all employees
are using the same tools to develop and measure knowledge growth

● Able to communicate centrally with every employee in a quick, easy and
meaningful way to share updates

● Contributes to overall employee development, satisfaction and
retention

**How to transform the way you train & communicate with your frontline
(that actually works)**

THE INDEPENDENT GROCER’S
GUIDE: WHAT IT IS, AND WHY NOW?
At UNFI, we believe that Independents are the heart and soul of the
grocery industry, and we stand on their side now more than ever.
For this reason, we asked AlixPartners – a professional service firm
that specializes in growth and operational excellence in grocery retail
and wholesale – to bring a perspective to independent retailers on
maximizing success post-pandemic. This Guide is the outcome of
their study; in it, you’ll find strategies that have contributed to many
Independents’ success.
• Their study is based on a mix of market research, industry expertise,
and in-person observation of best-in-class retailers.
We know that every Independent is unique and that no one knows
your customers or market better than you do.
At the same time, we found several common themes among successful
independents, which each applied in their way to their store(s). To that
end, we developed this Guide following two main guiding principles:
• To be successful, every independent needs a unique value
proposition for their customers. A store without a unique value
proposition is at risk of being out-competed by large chains.
• Although there isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution to success, there are
a few universal concepts and winning themes that Independents can
apply in a tailored way to their store(s) and customers.
Ultimately, we hope this Guide is a valuable resource for you to help
grow your business.
It doesn’t contain all of the answers, and you’ll find in here many things
you already do well today and others that might be new and helpful. As
you read through, you’ll need to decide which are most critical for you
and your customers and how to apply them to your unique business.

SG&A
Cost of executing
the promo event
Baseline
The amount of sales and margin the item makes at “Base” price
E.g., at $3.99, item A sells 30 units/week, making $45 in GM
Uplift
The incremental units sold when the item is in promotion
E.g., on the promo week, item A sells 10 more units per week
Vendor Funding
The contribution from suppliers to run the promotion
E.g., Vendor A provides $.80 rebate for each unit sold on promo
Halo
The additional sales driven by the promotion of the item
E.g., Ben comes to the store to buy item A, and buys also item C
Discount
The price discount required to achieve the promotional uplift
E.g., on promotion we reduce item A price by $1.00 to $2.99
Cannibalization
The sales lost due to shopper switching to the item in promo
E.g., Ben usually buys item B at $3.49. He buys item A instead
Pull-forward
The future sales lost on the item due to stock ups
E.g., Mary usually buys 1 unit per week. She buys 3 this week
Store Costs
The additional cost to execute the promo event
E.g., incremental labor in store to change the price tag

# Audio Restoration Strategy: Interview Denoising with Child Vocalization Removal

## Executive Summary
This document outlines a comprehensive, multi-stage approach for removing persistent high-pitched child vocalizations (screaming, crying, and other disruptive sounds) from the "Jock" interview recording. The strategy leverages the existing wavelet-based denoising implementation while incorporating advanced spectral processing, adaptive filtering, and AI-based source separation techniques.

## Available Resources
- **Primary Recording**: `jock_itntvw.wav` - Interview with subject "Jock" contaminated with child vocalizations
- **Noise Profile**: `evilhild_2.wav` - Isolated sample of unwanted child sounds for noise profiling
- **Existing Tools**: Python-based wavelet denoising implementation using PyWavelets

---

## Phase 1: Initial Analysis and Preparation

### 1.1 Audio File Assessment
```python
# Analyze both files for spectral characteristics
import soundfile as sf
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

# Load files
interview_data, interview_rate = sf.read('jock_itntvw.wav')
```

### 2.2 Spectral Subtraction Enhancement
Apply frequency-domain noise reduction using the noise profile:

```python
def spectral_subtraction(signal_fft, noise_profile_fft, alpha=2.0, beta=0.1):
    """
    Enhanced spectral subtraction with over-subtraction factor
    
    Parameters:
    - alpha: Over-subtraction factor (1.5-3.0 for aggressive removal)
    - beta: Spectral floor parameter (0.05-0.2 to prevent over-suppression)
    """
    magnitude = np.abs(signal_fft)
    phase = np.angle(signal_fft)
    noise_magnitude = np.abs(noise_profile_fft)
    
    # Apply subtraction with floor
    clean_magnitude = magnitude - alpha * noise_magnitude
    clean_magnitude = np.maximum(clean_magnitude, beta * magnitude)
    
    # Reconstruct signal
    return clean_magnitude * np.exp(1j * phase)
```

**Recommended Parameters:**
- **FFT Size**: 2048 samples (46ms @ 44.1kHz)
- **Overlap**: 75% for smooth reconstruction
- **Alpha (over-subtraction)**: 2.0-2.5 for child vocalizations
- **Beta (spectral floor)**: 0.1 to preserve speech naturalness

### 2.3 Adaptive Wiener Filtering
Implement frequency-dependent gain adjustment:

```python
def wiener_filter(noisy_spectrum, noise_power_spectrum, speech_power_estimate):
    """
    Adaptive Wiener filter for speech enhancement
    """
    snr_estimate = speech_power_estimate / (noise_power_spectrum + 1e-10)
    wiener_gain = snr_estimate / (1 + snr_estimate)
    
    # Apply frequency-dependent smoothing
    wiener_gain = signal.medfilt(wiener_gain, kernel_size=5)
    
    return noisy_spectrum * wiener_gain
```

### 3.3 Frequency-Specific Noise Gating
Target child vocalization frequency bands:

```python
def frequency_gate(signal_fft, gate_frequencies, threshold_db=-40):
    """
    Apply gating to specific frequency bands
    
    Gate Frequencies for Child Vocalizations:
    - Crying fundamental: 300-600 Hz
    - Screaming: 1000-3000 Hz
    - Harmonics: 2000-4000 Hz
    """
    magnitude = np.abs(signal_fft)
    magnitude_db = 20 * np.log10(magnitude + 1e-10)
    
    for freq_range in gate_frequencies:
        freq_mask = (frequencies >= freq_range[0]) & (frequencies <= freq_range[1])
        gate_mask = magnitude_db[freq_mask] < threshold_db
        magnitude[freq_mask][gate_mask] *= 0.1  # Aggressive attenuation
    
    return magnitude * np.exp(1j * np.angle(signal_fft))
```

**Recommended Gate Bands:**
- 300-600 Hz: Crying fundamental (threshold: -35 dB)
- 1000-3000 Hz: Screaming range (threshold: -40 dB)
- 3000-4000 Hz: High harmonics (threshold: -45 dB)

## Phase 4: Quality Control and Artifact Management

### 4.1 Musical Noise Suppression
Address spectral subtraction artifacts:

```python
def musical_noise_suppression(spectrum, smoothing_factor=0.98):
    """
    Temporal smoothing to reduce musical noise
    """
    # Apply recursive averaging
    smoothed = spectrum.copy()
    for i in range(1, len(spectrum)):
        smoothed[i] = smoothing_factor * smoothed[i-1] + \
                     (1 - smoothing_factor) * spectrum[i]
    return smoothed
```

### 4.2 Pumping Effect Mitigation
Prevent amplitude modulation artifacts:

```python
def anti_pumping_filter(gain_curve, attack_time=0.005, release_time=0.05):
    """
    Smooth gain transitions to prevent pumping
    
    Parameters:
    - attack_time: 5ms for quick response to speech
    - release_time: 50ms for smooth noise suppression
    """
    sample_rate = 44100
    attack_samples = int(attack_time * sample_rate)
    release_samples = int(release_time * sample_rate)
    
    smoothed_gain = np.zeros_like(gain_curve)
    
    for i in range(len(gain_curve)):
        if gain_curve[i] > smoothed_gain[i-1]:
            # Attack (fast)
            alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-1.0 / attack_samples)
        else:
            # Release (slow)
            alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-1.0 / release_samples)
        
        smoothed_gain[i] = alpha * gain_curve[i] + (1 - alpha) * smoothed_gain[i-1]
    
    return smoothed_gain
```

### 4.3 Frequency Masking Prevention
Preserve speech intelligibility:

```python
def preserve_formants(processed_spectrum, original_spectrum, formant_frequencies):
    """
    Protect speech formants from over-processing
    
    Typical Formant Ranges:
    - F1: 300-900 Hz
    - F2: 900-2500 Hz
    - F3: 2500-3500 Hz
    """
    protected_spectrum = processed_spectrum.copy()
    
    for f_range in formant_frequencies:
        freq_mask = (frequencies >= f_range[0]) & (frequencies <= f_range[1])
        # Blend processed and original in formant regions
        protected_spectrum[freq_mask] = 0.7 * processed_spectrum[freq_mask] + \
                                       0.3 * original_spectrum[freq_mask]
    
    return protected_spectrum
```

### 5.1 Multi-band Compression
Balance frequency ranges post-denoising:

```python
from scipy.signal import butter, sosfilt

def multiband_compress(audio, sample_rate=44100):
    """
    4-band compression for final polish
    """
    bands = [
        (20, 250),      # Sub-bass/bass
        (250, 1000),    # Low-mids
        (1000, 4000),   # High-mids (critical for speech)
        (4000, 20000)   # Highs
    ]
    
    compressed_bands = []
    for low, high in bands:
        sos = butter(4, [low, high], btype='band', fs=sample_rate, output='sos')
        band_signal = sosfilt(sos, audio)
        
        # Apply band-specific compression
        if low == 1000:  # Speech-critical band
            ratio = 2:1
            threshold = -20
        else:
            ratio = 3:1
            threshold = -25
            
        compressed_bands.append(compress(band_signal, ratio, threshold))
    
    return np.sum(compressed_bands, axis=0)
```

### 5.2 Adaptive EQ Restoration
Compensate for frequency loss:

```python
def adaptive_eq(processed_audio, reference_spectrum):
    """
    Match spectral envelope to reference
    """
    # Calculate spectral tilt correction
    processed_spectrum = np.fft.rfft(processed_audio)
    
    # Design compensation filter
    compensation_curve = reference_spectrum / (np.abs(processed_spectrum) + 1e-10)
    compensation_curve = np.clip(compensation_curve, 0.5, 2.0)  # Limit boost/cut
    
    # Apply smooth EQ curve
    from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter1d
    smooth_curve = gaussian_filter1d(compensation_curve, sigma=5)
    
    return np.fft.irfft(processed_spectrum * smooth_curve)
```

### 5.3 Final Limiting and Normalization
```python
def final_master(audio, target_lufs=-16):
    """
    Final stage mastering
    """
    # Peak limiting
    limited = np.tanh(audio * 0.9) / 0.9  # Soft saturation limiter
    
    # LUFS normalization
    import pyloudnorm as pyln
    meter = pyln.Meter(44100)
    loudness = meter.integrated_loudness(limited)
    normalized = pyln.normalize.loudness(limited, loudness, target_lufs)
    
    return normalized
```

### Strategy C: Segment-Based Processing
```python
def segment_based_processing(audio, segment_duration=1.0):
    """
    Apply different processing based on segment characteristics
    """
    segments = []
    segment_samples = int(segment_duration * sample_rate)
    
    for i in range(0, len(audio), segment_samples):
        segment = audio[i:i+segment_samples]
        
        # Analyze segment
        has_speech = detect_voice_activity(segment)
        noise_level = estimate_noise_level(segment)
        
        # Apply appropriate processing
        if has_speech and noise_level > threshold:
            processed = aggressive_denoise(segment)
        elif has_speech:
            processed = moderate_denoise(segment)
        else:
            processed = noise_gate(segment)
            
        segments.append(processed)
    
    return np.concatenate(segments)
```

"""
This class has two main functions

    - De-noising the file (pywt does it)
    - Creating a Noise Profile (parses the signal and creates a profile very memory heavy)
"""

import numpy as np
import pywt
import soundfile
from tqdm import tqdm

from lib.noiseProfiler import NoiseProfiler


def mad(arr):
    """ Median Absolute Deviation: a "Robust" version of standard deviation.
        Indices variability of the sample.
        https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_absolute_deviation 
    """
    arr = np.ma.array(arr).compressed()
    med = np.median(arr)
    return np.median(np.abs(arr - med))


class AudioDeNoise:
    """
    Class to de-noise the audio signal. The audio file is read in chunks and processed,
    cleaned and appended to the output file..

    It can de-noise multiple channels, any sized file, formats supported by soundfile

    Wavelets used ::
        Daubechies 4 : db4
        Level : decided by pyWavelets

    Attributes
    ----------
    __inputFile : str
        name of the input audio file

    Examples
    --------
    To de noise an audio file

    >>> audioDenoiser = AudioDeNoise("input.wav")
    >>> audioDenoiser.deNoise("input_denoised.wav")

    To generate the noise profile

    >>> audioDenoiser = AudioDeNoise("input.wav")
    >>> audioDenoiser.generateNoiseProfile("input_noise_profile.wav")
    """

    def __init__(self, inputFile):
        self.__inputFile = inputFile
        self.__noiseProfile = None

    def deNoise(self, outputFile):
        """
        De-noising function that reads the audio signal in chunks and processes
        and writes to the output file efficiently.

        VISU Shrink is used to generate the noise threshold

        Parameters
        ----------
        outputFile : str
            de-noised file name

        """
        info = soundfile.info(self.__inputFile)  # getting info of the audio
        rate = info.samplerate

        with soundfile.SoundFile(outputFile, "w", samplerate=rate, channels=info.channels) as of:
            for block in tqdm(soundfile.blocks(self.__inputFile, int(rate * info.duration * 0.10))):
                coefficients = pywt.wavedec(block, 'db4', mode='per', level=2)

                #  getting variance of the input signal
                sigma = mad(coefficients[- 1])

                # VISU Shrink thresholding by applying the universal threshold proposed by Donoho and Johnstone
                thresh = sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.log(len(block)))

                # thresholding using the noise threshold generated
                coefficients[1:] = (pywt.threshold(i, value=thresh, mode='soft') for i in coefficients[1:])

                # getting the clean signal as in original form and writing to the file
                clean = pywt.waverec(coefficients, 'db4', mode='per')
                of.write(clean)

    def generateNoiseProfile(self, noiseFile):
        """
        Parses the input signal and generate the noise profile using wavelet helper
        Look into lib modules to see how the parsing is done

        NOTE: Heavy on the memory, suitable for small files.

        Parameters
        ----------
        noiseFile : str
            name for the noise signal extracted
        """
        data, rate = soundfile.read(noiseFile)
        self.__noiseProfile = NoiseProfiler(data)
        noiseSignal = self.__noiseProfile.getNoiseDataPredicted()

        soundfile.write(noiseFile, noiseSignal, rate)

    def __del__(self):
        """
        clean up
        """
        del self.__noiseProfile

# Audio De-noising 
A simple yet very powerful noise remover and reducer built in python.
The noise removed by using Wavelet Transform.

Wavelets has been very powerful tool to decompose the audio signal into parts and apply thresholds to eliminate
unwanted signal like noise. The thresholding method is the most important in the process of Audio De nosing.

The thresholding used is VisuShrink method or the universal threshold introduce by Donoho

This repo uses `pywt`. I have a custom implementation of wavelet here [wavelets](https://github.com/AP-Atul/wavelets) & [wavelets-ext](https://github.com/AP-Atul/wavelets-ext) (cython speed up)


## Execution
- Install the dependencies
    ```$ pip3 install -r requirements.txt```
- Use the denoise.py file
    ```python
    from denoise import AudioDeNoise 
    
    audioDenoiser = AudioDeNoise(inputFile="input.wav")
    audioDenoiser.deNoise(outputFile="input_denoised.wav")
    audioDenoiser.generateNoiseProfile(noiseFile="input_noise_profile.wav")
    ```

# Audio Restoration Pipeline - Production-Grade System

A comprehensive 6-phase audio restoration pipeline for removing persistent background noise (specifically child vocalizations) from interview recordings, with deterministic processing, optional AI enhancement, and professional mastering.

## Features

- **6-Phase Processing Pipeline**:
  1. **Analysis & Noise Profiling**: Spectral analysis, VAD, child-band detection
  2. **Primary Noise Reduction**: Wavelet denoising, spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering
  3. **HPSS**: Harmonic-Percussive Source Separation
  4. **AI Enhancement** (Optional): Demucs, Spleeter, SpeechBrain integration
  5. **Artifact Control**: Click removal, musical noise suppression, phase coherence
  6. **Mastering**: LUFS normalization, true-peak limiting, multiband compression

- **Production Features**:
  - Deterministic seeding for reproducibility
  - Dry-run mode for planning
  - Strict mode for CI/CD
  - Comprehensive logging and metrics
  - Run manifest with provenance tracking
  - Multiple config profiles

## Quick Start

### 1. Installation

```bash
# Clone repository
git clone <repository>
cd Audio-Denoising

# Install minimal dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install pyyaml

# Optional: Install AI dependencies
pip install -r ai-extras.txt
pip install demucs spleeter  # For AI source separation
```

### 2. Basic Usage

```bash
# Run core denoising (Phases 1-2 only)
make run-core INPUT=jock_itntvw.wav NOISE=evilhild_2.wav

# Run full pipeline without AI (Phases 1-3, 5-6)
make run-full

# Run complete pipeline with AI (all phases)
make install-ai  # First time only
make run-ai
```

### 3. Using Python Directly

```bash
# Core pipeline
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/core_only.yaml --phases 1,2

# Full pipeline
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --phases all

# With AI
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_with_ai.yaml --phases all

# Dry run to test
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --phases all --dry-run
```

## Configuration

Three pre-configured profiles are provided:

### 1. `configs/core_only.yaml`
- Phases 1-2 only
- Basic wavelet denoising + spectral methods
- Fastest processing
- No external dependencies

### 2. `configs/full_no_ai.yaml`
- All phases except AI (Phase 4 disabled)
- HPSS, artifact control, mastering
- Quality metrics evaluation
- No AI dependencies required

### 3. `configs/full_with_ai.yaml`
- All phases including AI enhancement
- Demucs/Spleeter for source separation
- Speech enhancement with SpeechBrain
- Requires `ai-extras.txt` installation

### 4. `configs/full_pipeline.yaml`
- Complete configuration reference
- All parameters exposed
- Extensive comments
- Use as template for custom configs

## Pipeline Phases

### Phase 1: Analysis & Noise Profile
```python
# Analyzes audio characteristics
python src/analyze_audio.py --config <config>

# Learns noise profile from sample
python src/noise_profile.py --config <config>
```
- Generates spectrograms
- Detects child vocalization bands (300-600Hz, 1-3kHz, 3-4kHz)
- Creates time-varying noise profile

### Phase 2: Primary Noise Reduction
```python
# Wavelet denoising
python src/wavelet_denoise.py --config <config>

# Spectral subtraction
python src/spectral_subtract.py --config <config>

# Wiener filtering
python src/wiener_filter.py --config <config>
```
- VisuShrink wavelet thresholding
- Alpha/beta spectral subtraction
- VAD-guided Wiener filtering

### Phase 3: HPSS
```python
python src/hpss_separate.py --config <config>
```
- Separates harmonic (speech) from percussive (noise)
- Median filtering or librosa methods
- Preserves transients

### Phase 4: AI Enhancement (Optional)
```python
python src/ai_separate.py --config <config>
```
- **Demucs**: Neural source separation
- **Spleeter**: Fast vocal isolation
- **SpeechBrain**: Speech enhancement
- Falls back to classical methods if unavailable

### Phase 5: Artifact Control
```python
python src/artifact_control.py --config <config>
```
- Click/pop removal
- Musical noise suppression
- Pre-echo control
- De-essing
- Phase coherence (Griffin-Lim)
- Safety limiting

### Phase 6: Mastering
```python
python src/mastering_chain.py --config <config> --profile streaming
```
Profiles available:
- **streaming**: -14 LUFS (Spotify/Apple Music)
- **podcast**: -16 LUFS
- **broadcast**: -23 LUFS (EBU R128)
- **club**: -9 LUFS

Features:
- LUFS normalization
- True-peak limiting
- Multiband compression
- Tilt EQ
- Dithering with noise shaping

### Metrics Evaluation
```python
python src/metrics_eval.py --config <config> --reference clean.wav
```
Computes:
- SNR improvement
- PESQ (speech quality)
- STOI (intelligibility)
- SI-SDR
- Log-spectral distance

## Advanced Usage

### Dry Run Mode
Test pipeline without processing:
```bash
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --dry-run
```

### Strict Mode
Fail on missing dependencies (for CI/CD):
```bash
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --strict
```

### Custom Phase Selection
Run specific phases:
```bash
# Only analysis and HPSS
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --phases 1,3

# Skip mastering
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --phases 1,2,3,4,5,metrics
```

### Override Inputs
```bash
python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml \
    --input my_audio.wav \
    --noise my_noise.wav \
    --reference clean_reference.wav
```

## Metrics & Quality Targets

| Metric | Target | Description |
|--------|--------|-------------|
| SNR Improvement | >15 dB | Signal-to-noise ratio gain |
| PESQ | >3.5 | Perceptual speech quality (1-5) |
| STOI | >0.85 | Short-time objective intelligibility (0-1) |
| SI-SDR | >10 dB | Scale-invariant signal-to-distortion |
| LUFS | -16±0.5 | Integrated loudness (podcast) |
| True Peak | <-1 dBTP | Maximum true peak level |

## Troubleshooting

### Common Issues

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| ModuleNotFoundError: demucs | Install AI extras: `pip install -r ai-extras.txt` |
| PESQ/STOI unavailable | Install metrics: `pip install pesq pystoi` |
| Robotic/metallic voice | Reduce spectral_subtraction.alpha to 1.8 |
| Pumping/breathing | Increase wiener.release_ms to 100 |
| Musical noise | Enable artifact_control.musical_noise |
| Residual child noise | Increase spectral_subtraction.alpha to 2.5 |

### Performance Optimization

For faster processing:
1. Disable unused phases in config
2. Reduce HPSS iterations
3. Skip metrics evaluation during testing
4. Use `phase4.ai_enhancement.speech_enhancement.chunk_size_sec: 30`

For better quality:
1. Enable all artifact control features
2. Increase Griffin-Lim iterations to 64
3. Use Demucs with shifts=5
4. Enable multiband HPSS

### GPU Acceleration

For AI phases with CUDA:
```yaml
ai_enhancement:
  demucs:
    device: cuda
  speech_enhancement:
    device: cuda
```

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""
Test script to verify individual phases of the audio restoration pipeline
Run this to test each phase in isolation before running the full pipeline
"""
import os
import sys
import subprocess
import argparse
from pathlib import Path

def run_command(cmd, description):
    """Run a command and report results"""
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"Testing: {description}")
    print(f"Command: {cmd}")
    print('='*60)
    
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
        if result.returncode == 0:
            print(f"✅ SUCCESS: {description}")
            if result.stdout:
                print("Output:", result.stdout[:500])  # First 500 chars
        else:
            print(f"❌ FAILED: {description}")
            print("Error:", result.stderr[:1000])  # First 1000 chars of error
        return result.returncode == 0
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"❌ EXCEPTION: {e}")
        return False

def test_phase(phase_num, script_name, config_file="configs/full_no_ai.yaml"):
    """Test a single phase"""
    cmd = f"python src/{script_name} --config {config_file}"
    return run_command(cmd, f"Phase {phase_num}: {script_name}")

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Test individual pipeline phases")
    parser.add_argument("--phase", type=int, help="Test specific phase (1-6)")
    parser.add_argument("--config", default="configs/full_no_ai.yaml", 
                       help="Config file to use")
    parser.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", 
                       help="Test all phases sequentially")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    # Phase definitions
    phases = {
        1: ("analyze_audio.py", "Audio Analysis"),
        2: ("noise_profile.py", "Noise Profile Learning"),
        3: ("hpss_separate.py", "HPSS Separation"),
        4: ("ai_separate.py", "AI Enhancement"),
        5: ("artifact_control.py", "Artifact Control"),
        6: ("mastering_chain.py", "Mastering Chain")
    }
    
    # Additional phase 2 sub-phases
    phase2_scripts = [
        ("wavelet_denoise.py", "Wavelet Denoising"),
        ("spectral_subtract.py", "Spectral Subtraction"),
        ("wiener_filter.py", "Wiener Filtering")
    ]
    
    results = {}
    
    if args.all:
        # Test all phases
        print("\n" + "="*60)
        print("TESTING ALL PHASES")
        print("="*60)
        
        # Phase 1
        success = test_phase(1, phases[1][0], args.config)
        results["Phase 1"] = success
        
        # Phase 2 (multiple scripts)
        if success:
            success = test_phase("2a", phases[2][0], args.config)
            results["Phase 2a"] = success
            
            for script, desc in phase2_scripts:
                if success:
                    success = test_phase(f"2-{script.split('.')[0]}", script, args.config)
                    results[f"Phase 2-{desc}"] = success
        
        # Phases 3-6
        for phase_num in range(3, 7):
            if success or phase_num == 3:  # Continue even if phase 2 fails
                success = test_phase(phase_num, phases[phase_num][0], args.config)
                results[f"Phase {phase_num}"] = success
        
        # Metrics evaluation
        if success:
            cmd = "python src/metrics_eval.py --config " + args.config
            success = run_command(cmd, "Metrics Evaluation")
            results["Metrics"] = success
        
    elif args.phase:
        # Test specific phase
        if args.phase == 2:
            # Test all phase 2 scripts
            success = test_phase("2a", phases[2][0], args.config)
            results["Phase 2a"] = success
            
            for script, desc in phase2_scripts:
                success = test_phase(f"2-{script.split('.')[0]}", script, args.config)
                results[f"Phase 2-{desc}"] = success
        elif args.phase in phases:
            success = test_phase(args.phase, phases[args.phase][0], args.config)
            results[f"Phase {args.phase}"] = success
        else:
            print(f"Invalid phase number: {args.phase}")
            return
    else:
        print("Please specify --phase N or --all")
        parser.print_help()
        return
    
    # Summary
    print("\n" + "="*60)
    print("TEST SUMMARY")
    print("="*60)
    
    for phase, success in results.items():
        status = "✅ PASS" if success else "❌ FAIL"
        print(f"{phase}: {status}")
    
    total = len(results)
    passed = sum(1 for s in results.values() if s)
    print(f"\nTotal: {passed}/{total} phases passed")
    
    if passed == total:
        print("\n🎉 All tests passed! Ready to run full pipeline:")
        print("  python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --phases all")
    else:
        print("\n⚠️ Some tests failed. Please check the errors above.")
        print("You can still run phases 1-2 with:")
        print("  python src/pipeline_v2.py --config configs/full_no_ai.yaml --phases 1,2")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is an easier way for many devices
to set up a secure Wi-Fi network connection. Instead of manually
entering passwords or multiple keys on each Wi-Fi client, such as a
laptop, printer, or external hard drive, your Verizon Internet Gateway
creates a secure Wi-Fi network connection.
In most cases, this only requires the pressing of two buttons – one
on your Verizon Internet Gateway and one on the Wi-Fi client.
This could be either a built-in button or one on a compatible Wi-Fi
adapter/card, or a virtual button in software. Once completed, this
allows Wi-Fi clients to join your Wi-Fi network.
To initialize the WPS process, you can either press and hold the
unified button located on the front of your Verizon Internet Gateway
for more than two seconds or use the UI and press the on-screen

3.0/ OVERVIEW
Your Verizon Internet Gateway provides you with Wi-Fi connectivity
using the 802.11a, b, g, n, ac or ax standards. These are the most
common Wi-Fi standards.
802.11b has a maximum data rate of 11 Mbps, 802.11a and 802.11g
have a maximum data rate of 54 Mbps, 802.11n has a maximum data
rate of 450 Mbps, 802.11ac has a maximum data rate of 3.12 Gbps,
and 802.11ax has a maximum data rate of 4.8 Gbps.
802.11b and g standards operate in the 2.4 GHz range. 802.11ac
operates in the 5 GHz range. 802.11n and ax operate in both the
2.4 GHz and 5 GHz ranges.
Note: 802.11a, 802.11b, and 802.11g are legacy modes and are not
recommended. Even one such device connected to the network will
slow your entire Wi-Fi network.
The Wi-Fi service and Wi-Fi security are activated by default. The
level of security is preset to WPA2 encryption using a unique default
WPA2 key (also referred to as a passphrase or password) pre-
configured at the factory. This information is displayed on a sticker
located on the bottom of your Verizon Internet Gateway.
Your Gateway integrates multiple layers of security. These include
Wi-Fi Protected Access, and firewall.

5.0/ SECURITY & FIREWALL
The firewall is the cornerstone of the security suite for your
Verizon Internet Gateway. It has been exclusively tailored to the
needs of the residential or office user and is pre-configured to
provide optimum security.
The firewall provides both the security and flexibility that home
and office users seek. It provides a managed, professional level
of network security while enabling the safe use of interactive
applications, such as internet gaming and video conferencing.
Additional features, including surfing restrictions and access
control, can also be configured locally through the user interface or
remotely by a service provider.
The firewall regulates the flow of data between the local
network and the internet. Both incoming and outgoing data are
inspected, then either accepted and allowed to pass through your
Verizon Internet Gateway or rejected and barred from passing
through your Verizon Internet Gateway, according to a flexible
and configurable set of rules. These rules are designed to prevent
unwanted intrusions from the outside, while allowing local network
users access to internet services.
The firewall rules specify the type of services on the internet that
are accessible from the local network and types of services in the
local network that are accessible from the internet.

SECURItY & FIREwall
Each request for a service that the firewall receives is checked
against the firewall rules to determine whether the request should
be allowed to pass through the firewall. If the request is permitted to
pass, all subsequent data associated with this request or session is
also allowed to pass, regardless of its direction.
For example, when accessing a website on the internet, a request
is sent to the internet for this site. When the request reaches your
Verizon Internet Gateway, the firewall identifies the request type and
origin, such as HTTP and a specific computer in the local network.
Unless your Verizon Internet Gateway is configured to block
requests of this type from this computer, the firewall allows this type
of request to pass to the internet.
When the website is returned from the web server, the firewall
associates the website with this session and allows it to pass;
regardless HTTP access from the internet to the local network is
blocked or permitted. It is the origin of the request, not subsequent
responses to this request, which determines whether a session can
be established.

5.0g/ PORT TRIGGERING
Port triggering can be described as dynamic port forwarding. By
setting port triggering rules, inbound traffic arrives at a specific
network host using ports that are different than those used for
outbound traffic. The outbound traffic triggers the ports where the
inbound traffic is directed.

81

For example, a gaming server is accessed using UDP protocol on
port 2222. The gaming server then responds by connecting the
user using UDP on port 3333, when a gaming session is initiated.
In this case, port triggering must be used since it conflicts with the
following default firewall settings:
• Firewall blocks inbound traffic by default.
• Server replies to your Verizon Internet Gateway IP, and the
connection is not sent back to the host since it is not part of a
session.
To resolve the conflict, a port triggering entry must be defined,
which allows inbound traffic on UDP port 3333 only after a
network host generated traffic to UDP port 2222. This results in
your Verizon Internet Gateway accepting the inbound traffic from
the gaming server and sending it back to the network host which
originated the outgoing traffic to UDP port 2222.
To configure port triggering:
1. From the AdvancedAdvanced menu, select Security & FirewallSecurity & Firewall and
then click Port TriggeringPort Triggering.

5.1d/ IPV4 ADDRESS DISTRIbUTION
You can easily add computers configured as DHCP clients to the
network. The DHCP server provides a mechanism for allocating IP
addresses to these hosts and for delivering network configuration
parameters to the hosts.
For example, a client (host) sends a broadcast message on the
network requesting an IP address for itself. The DHCP server
then checks its list of available addresses and leases a local IP
address to the host for a specific period of time and simultaneously
designates this IP address as taken. At this point, the host is
configured with an IP address for the duration of the lease.
The host can renew an expiring lease or let it expire. If it renews
a lease, the host receives current information about network
services, as it did during the original lease, allowing it to update its
network configurations to reflect any changes that occurred since
the first connection to the network.
If the host wishes to terminate a lease before its expiration, it
sends a release message to the DHCP server. This makes the IP
address available for use by other hosts.
The DHCP server performs the following functions:
• Displays a list of all DHCP host devices connected to your
Verizon Internet Gateway
• Defines the range of IP addresses that can be allocated in the
network
• Defines the length of time the dynamic IP addresses are
allocated

supply for a few minutes (3 or more) and then reconnect the power
cable.

6.0e/ LAN CONNECTION FAILURE
To troubleshoot a LAN connection failure:
• Verify your Verizon Internet Gateway is properly installed, LAN
connections are correct, and that the Verizon Internet Gateway
and communicating network devices are all powered on.
• Confirm that the computer and Verizon Internet Gateway are
both on the same network segment.
If unsure, let the computer get the IP address automatically by
initiating the DHCP function, then verify the computer is using an IP
address within the default range of 192.168.1.2 through 192.168.1.254.
If the computer is not using an IP address within the correct IP
range, it will not connect to your Verizon Internet Gateway.
• Verify the subnet mask address is set to 255.255.255.0.
6.0f/ TIMEOUT ERROR OCCURS WhEN ENTERING ThE URL OR
IP ADDRESS
Verify the following:
• All computers are working properly.
• IP settings are correct.
• Verizon Internet Gateway is on and connected properly.
• Verizon Internet Gateway settings are the same as the computer.

For connections experiencing lag or a slow response:
• Check for other devices on the network utilizing large portions
of the bandwidth and if possible temporarily stop their current
utilization and recheck the connection.
• If lag still exists, clear the cache on the computer and if
still needed, unplug the Ethernet cable or disable the Wi-Fi
connection to the computer experiencing the slow connection
and then reconnect or enable the Wi-Fi connection and try the
connection again.
In rare cases you may also need to:
• Unplug the Ethernet cable to Verizon Internet Gateway and
restart the Verizon Internet Gateway, wait 1-2 mins. and insert
the Ethernet cable again.

configuration on the router, based on the application you are
using (refer to the 5.0e/ Port Forwarding section or Verizon’s
support online help for more details).

6.1f/ CAN I USE AN OLDER WI-FI DEVICE TO CONNECT TO MY
VERIZON INTERNET GATEWAY?
Yes, your Verizon Internet Gateway can interface with 802.11b, g,
n, ac or ax devices. Your Verizon Internet Gateway also can be
setup to handle only n Wi-Fi cards, g Wi-Fi cards, b Wi-Fi cards,
or any combination of the three.

The physical environment surrounding your Verizon Internet
Gateway can have a varying effect on signal strength and quality.
The denser the object, such as a concrete wall compared to
a plaster wall, the greater the interference. Concrete or metal
reinforced structures experience a higher degree of signal loss
than those made of wood, plaster, or glass.

docs.content:
Planning a virtual documentary screening seemed like a fantastic idea. I envisioned a cozy online gathering for â€œGolden Wings: 50 Year Flight Pathâ€ where everyone could enjoy my latest work, blissfully unaware of the chaos that awaited me. Little did I know, my meticulous preparation would soon unravel into a tapestry of hilarious mishaps and frustrating roadblocks. Grab your popcorn, folksâ€”this is the tale of how I almost derailed my own premiere.

The Perfect Plan (Or So I Thought)
Three weeks before D-day, I launched a marketing blitz that would make Don Draper proud. Facebook, TikTok, Redditâ€”if it had a scroll feature, I was there, shouting into the digital void about my upcoming screening. The cherry on top? It was scheduled for my momâ€™s birthday. Sheâ€™d be in Japan, but she promised to join, adding a sprinkle of sentimentality to my grand vision.

Marketing Madness: The Molasses Effect

I marketed like a caffeinated squirrel, scattering ads across the internet with reckless abandon. But the sign-ups? They trickled in slower than molasses flowing uphill in January. Each ping of a new registration felt like a hard-won victory. Friends and family eventually rallied, bless their hearts, even if their numbers were more â€œintimate gatheringâ€ than â€œviral sensation.â€

Tech Troubles: When 8GB Feels Like 8KB
The big day arrived, and in a stroke of what I thought was genius, I decided to make a new cut of my documentary. My trusty MacBook Pro, armed with a modest 8GB of RAM, wheezed at the mere suggestion. Editing became a Herculean task, like trying to squeeze an elephant through a garden hose.

My poor MacBook, overwhelmed by the data onslaught, threw in the towel. It crashed more times than I care to count, spitting out videos that were either mute as a mime or glitchier than a scrambled cable channel circa 1995.


The Great RAM Upgrade: A Race Against Time
Realizing I needed more horsepower, I bit the bullet and ordered a new desktop with 16GB of RAM, with plans to upgrade to 32GB. Amazon promised the additional RAM would arrive the Friday before the screening. Spoiler alert: it didnâ€™t. The package finally graced my doorstep Sunday afternoon, mere hours before showtime.

DIY RAM Installation: Fumbling Towards Glory

Picture this: me, armed with a YouTube tutorial and a prayer, attempting to install RAM for the first time. My hands shook like I was defusing a bomb rather than upgrading a computer. For an agonizing hour, I fumbled with tiny screws and delicate components, feeling less like a tech wizard and more like Mr. Magoo in a microchip factory.

Miraculously, the computer booted up. I had done it! But my victory dance was short-livedâ€”I now had precious little time to finish editing.


Platform Panic: The Last-Minute Switch
T-minus one hour, and a horrifying realization struck: Zoom required downloads. My tech-challenged attendees would struggle more than a cat in a bathtub. Cue frantic platform switch to Google Meet.

This eleventh-hour change meant guiding my jet-lagged mom through setup from her hotel in Japan. Her Wi-Fi connection was spottier than a dalmatian, and her patience was wearing thinner than hotel toilet paper. But bless her, she persevered.

The Screening: Murphyâ€™s Law in Action
Finally, fashionably late by 30 minutes, the screening began. My audience? A whopping three people: my first-grade teacher (bless her supportive soul), my cousin (family obligation at its finest), and my momâ€™s high school friend (curiosity trumps convenience).

But wait! The universe wasnâ€™t done with me yet. The video streamed beautifullyâ€”a silent film for the modern age. No audio. Nada. Zip.

For ten excruciating minutes, I flailed at my computer like a cartoon character swatting flies. My audience watched in bemused silence as I morphed into a living embodiment of the buffering symbol.


The Silver Lining: A Birthday to Remember
Despite the technical tempest, a warm glow emerged. There was my mom, beaming from her hotel room in Japan, celebrating her birthday in the quirkiest way possible. My first-grade teacherâ€™s familiar smile brought a wave of nostalgia. And my momâ€™s high school friend? She got a front-row seat to a comedy of errors she never signed up for.

In the end, I admitted defeat gracefully(ish) and promised to send everyone a link to the rough cut. Not quite the premiere Iâ€™d envisioned, but a memorable one nonetheless.


Ending on a Sweet Note (Literally)
After the dust settled, I crafted an email to my loyal attendees and those who signed up but couldnâ€™t make it. It took me a good 30 minutes to write, each word carefully chosen and coming straight from the heart:

â€œWell, that was a hoot and a half!!

Thank you all for attending. It was very sweet. As an actor, I get these nightmares of being on stage in a play with no recollection of ever having rehearsed or learning any lines. Itâ€™s called the actorâ€™s nightmare, and Iâ€™ve yet to meet an actor who hasnâ€™t experienced it. I now know what the directorâ€™s nightmare is â€“ Iâ€™ve lived it. Itâ€™s inviting people to come see your work and then the movie not playing! LOL!

On the bright side, I got to see my Mom for her birthday. I also got to see my first-grade teacher Kathi, cousin Kathy and Gene, and meet Paula! Thanks again to all of you.

Iâ€™m including the Google Drive link to the full rough cut of the documentary.

The only thing I ask is that you watch it because my Mom was so incredibly brave and let herself become vulnerable in front of the camera. The heart of any good documentary is truth, and you see something real here. My motherâ€™s bravery, humility, and good humor are all on display in this film. It is moving and captivating, and I plan on showing it to the world!

To those of you who could not attend, Iâ€™m sending you the link as well. It was my fault we got started late, so you should get to see it too. Itâ€™s a rough world out there, so letâ€™s all try to make it a better place while we have the gift of being here.

Warmest regards,

Caleb Mills Stewartâ€

As soon as I finished writing, I called my mom to read it to her. I couldnâ€™t make it through without my voice cracking and tears welling up. She told me it was beautiful and that she thought it was a wonderful birthday present, technical difficulties and all. Her words meant the world to me.

The Emotional Undercurrent

As I reflect on this experience, I realize that my emotional response wasnâ€™t just about the screening. Iâ€™m currently remastering the ending of the documentary, which deals with a deeply personal event: my Dadâ€™s sudden passing while my Mom was on duty in Frankfurt.

Itâ€™s been ten years, but the grief is still there, a constant companion that ebbs and flows. Most days, I think of him with a smile, remembering his patience, wisdom, and love for laughter. Other times, like now, I find myself misty-eyed, wondering what he would say about my latest project.

I was one of the lucky ones, gifted with a wonderful father. His laugh was infectious, a sound Iâ€™d give anything to hear just one more time. Miss you, Dad. Love you.

Conclusion: A Screening to Remember
While my virtual screening didnâ€™t go as planned, it became so much more than just a premiere. It was a roller coaster of emotions, a test of resilience, and a reminder of what truly matters. The technical glitches and low turnout fade in importance when I think about connecting with my mom on her birthday, reuniting with my first-grade teacher, and feeling my dadâ€™s presence in the work Iâ€™m doing.

Henry and Robyn Stewart dressed up for an anniversary dinner circa 1986
Henry and Robyn Stewart as featured in â€œGolden Wingsâ€
This experience taught me valuable lessons about filmmaking, sure, but more importantly, it reminded me of the power of vulnerability, the strength of family bonds, and the unexpected ways our loved ones continue to shape our lives.

Next time, Iâ€™ll be better prepared for the technical challenges, more flexible in my approach, and maybe â€“ just maybe â€“ Iâ€™ll crack the code of getting more sign-ups. But no matter what happens, Iâ€™ll carry with me the knowledge that itâ€™s not about perfect executions or massive audiences. Itâ€™s about the stories we tell, the connections we make, and the love we share.

And that, technical difficulties and all, is worth every moment of effort.


Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
(Or as I like to call them, â€œFrightfully Awkward Quandariesâ€)

1. What inspired you to create â€œGolden Wings: Fifty Year Flight Pathâ€? Was it a sudden desire to become the Scorsese of the skies?

Picture this: There I was in graduate school, enrolled in a documentary filmmaking class, probably wearing a beret and pretending to understand French New Wave cinema. Our final assignment was to create a 10-minute documentary. Being the brilliant strategist that I am, I thought, â€œAha! Iâ€™ll take the easy way out and make a doc about my momâ€™s 53-year career as a flight attendant!â€

Spoiler alert: It was about as â€œeasyâ€ as trying to fit a Boeing 747 into a parking spot at the mall. Iâ€™d unknowingly signed up for the filmmaking equivalent of an ultra-marathonâ€¦ in flip-flopsâ€¦ uphillâ€¦ both ways. But hey, sometimes taking the â€œeasyâ€ way out is just lifeâ€™s way of tricking you into doing something amazing. How delightfully, frustratingly human of me!

2. How do you handle technical difficulties during screenings? Interpretive dance? Smoke signals? Carrier pigeons?

First step: Resist the urge to have a full-blown, toddler-style meltdown in front of your audience. Save that for later, preferably in the privacy of your car or a large, soundproof closet.

Second: Channel your inner swan â€“ all grace and poise on the surface, while paddling frantically underneath. Apologize to your audience with the smoothness of a used car salesman and the sincerity of a golden retriever.

If all else fails, have a backup plan. Mine was to give everyone a link to the rough cut of the documentary. Itâ€™s not password protected because apparently, I like to live dangerously. Or I trust people. Or both.

Remember: If you canâ€™t give them a show, at least give them a story to tell at parties!

3. What are your top tips for marketing a virtual event? Wrong answers only, please.

Well, folks, gather â€™round for a masterclass in â€œWhat Not To Do in Marketing 101.â€ First tip: Cast a net so wide, youâ€™re basically fishing in the Sahara.

I focused on Facebook with the dedication of a cat ignoring its expensive new toy. Spoiler: It worked about as well as using a flyswatter to catch a whale.

Then there was Reddit, where I got more engagement than a ring shop on Valentineâ€™s Day, but about as many sign-ups as a voluntary tax seminar.

My eyes were bigger than my â€œdigital stomachâ€ â€“ a metaphor so bad, itâ€™s probably causing English teachers worldwide to wake up in a cold sweat.

Pro tip: If you want to learn about marketing, just do the opposite of whatever I did. Youâ€™ll be fine!


4. How do you stay motivated during challenging projects? Caffeine? Inspirational cat posters? Interpretive screaming?

Ah, motivation â€“ that elusive unicorn of productivity. My secret? I try to remain reflective, which is a fancy way of saying I stare at myself in the mirror and ask, â€œWhy? Why did you do this to yourself?â€

I also take breaks when needed, even though I feel guiltier than someone eating the last slice of pizza without offering to share. But sometimes, you need to step back and look at the bigger picture. Itâ€™s like trying to solve a 1000-piece jigsaw puzzle of the sky â€“ at some point, you need to stop staring at that one blue piece and remember thereâ€™s a whole image youâ€™re working towards.

Remember: Itâ€™s not a sprint, itâ€™s a marathon. A never-ending marathon. With hurdles. And maybe some quicksand. But hey, at least the scenery is interesting!

5. Whatâ€™s next for you in your filmmaking career? Planning to document the secret lives of airline peanuts, perhaps?

Well, first on the agenda is actually finishing â€œGolden Wings: Fifty Year Flight Path.â€ I know, wild concept, right? Finishing what I started? Revolutionary!

After that, Iâ€™m diving into new projects faster than a kid cannonballing into a pool on the first day of summer. Iâ€™m talking new stories, new techniques, maybe even figuring out which end of the camera to point at the subject!

If â€œGolden Wingsâ€ takes off (pun absolutely intended), I might expand it into a feature-length documentary. Think of it as â€œGolden Wings: Now With Extra Legroom.â€ Weâ€™ll explore more stories from the friendly skies, like:

The great airline deregulation: Or as I like to call it, â€œThe Day the Peanuts Stopped Being Freeâ€
The impact of the AIDS crisis on the flight attendant community: A heartbreaking but important chapter
The strikes of the early â€™90s: Because nothing says â€œjob satisfactionâ€ like standing on a picket line in uncomfortable shoes
So buckle up, keep your tray tables in their upright and locked position, and stay tuned. This filmmakerâ€™s career is cleared for takeoff!

GOLDEN WINGS TRANSCRIPT
00:00:09:12 - 00:00:42:12

Caleb Mills Stewart
Welcome aboard this special flight of Golden Wings. This is your director, Caleb Mills Stewart speaking. While pilots must retire at age 65. Flight attendants can score as long as their wings allow for 53 years. My mother, Robyn Stewart, has done just that through industry turbulence and personal challenges. She's remained airborne. So please fasten your seat belts and prepare for a multi-generational journey through time, all at 30,000ft.

00:00:42:14 - 00:01:09:16
Caleb Mills Stewart
Thank you for joining us. And enjoy the film.

00:01:09:18 - 00:02:00:13
Robyn Stewart
My name is Robyn Stewart, and I'm a flight attendant for American Airlines. I have been applying for American Airlines since 1971. So that's 52 years. I wanted to become a flight attendant because I wanted to fly free. I've been used to flying free with because my dad was was flying for American Airlines when I was a young child, and we were able to go on so many fun trips, and I wanted to continue to do that.

00:02:00:15 - 00:02:09:04
Robyn Stewart
My favorite thing about flying is going wherever I want.

00:02:09:06 - 00:02:09:19
Robyn Stewart
I went to.

00:02:09:19 - 00:02:19:20
Robyn Stewart
Rome last week. I'm going to run again next week.

00:02:19:22 - 00:02:31:21
Robyn Stewart
And the following week, I'll be going to Tokyo.

00:02:31:23 - 00:02:44:06
Robyn Stewart
Frankfurt, Germany.

00:02:44:08 - 00:03:16:16
Robyn Stewart
So, because I have the seniority that I have, I can pick and choose my schedule. And it's taken me a long time to get here, but it's been worth it.

00:03:16:18 - 00:03:19:11
Caleb Mills Stewart
Did you think that you'd be a flight attendant for 50 years when you started?

00:03:19:12 - 00:03:51:02
Robyn Stewart
Oh, no. I did not think I'll be a flight attendant more than 2 to 5 years. Well, I was hired. We had to be a certain way. We could not go over a weight limit. We had to wear girdles. We were subject to girdle checks. We were also subject to a parent's checks to make sure we had our makeup done right and our hair done and our nails done.

00:03:51:04 - 00:04:36:20
Robyn Stewart
They stopped doing girdle checks. Not long after I graduated in 1971. When I graduated. I was issued a stewardess manual, but that changed. # Documentary Analysis: Golden Wings: 50 Year Flight Path

## Narrative Structure

The documentary employs a sophisticated multi-layered narrative structure that weaves together several key storylines:

1. **Frame Narrative**
- Opens with a creative "flight announcement" metaphor from the director
- Establishes both the personal and professional aspects of the story
- Bookends with an emotional letter to his late father

2. **Historical Timeline**
- Chronicles the evolution of commercial aviation from the 1960s through present day
- Uses specific aircraft (707, 727, 747) as temporal markers
- Integrates industry changes with personal milestones

3. **Personal Journey Threads**
- Robyn Stewart's 50+ year career
- Jay Ricks' (grandfather) technical contributions
- Family dynamics across three generations
- Personal challenges and transformation

The structure effectively uses temporal shifts, moving between past and present, while maintaining clear narrative coherence through thematic connections.

## Key Themes and Messages

1. **Legacy and Generational Connection**
- The 747 serves as a symbolic bridge between generations
- Technical expertise passed down through family
- Aviation as family heritage

2. **Industry Evolution**
- Changes in airline culture (weight requirements, gender roles)
- Technological advancement (from 707 to 747)
- Post-9/11 transformation of air travel

3. **Personal Growth and Redemption**
- Robyn's journey through alcoholism to recovery
- American Airlines' role in supporting recovery
- The intersection of personal and professional life

4. **Love and Loss**
- The impact of Henry Stewart's death
- Community support during crisis
- The power of unconditional love (revealed in final letter)

5. **Breaking Barriers**
- Gender roles in aviation
- Changing perceptions of flight attendants
- Age and longevity in the profession

## Technical Execution

### Strengths
1. **Innovative Transitions**
- Creative use of aircraft sounds and visual metaphors
- Effective integration of archival footage
- Powerful use of silence and sound design (especially during 9/11 sequence)

2. **Interview Technique**
- Intimate, conversational style between mother and son
- Natural flow that allows for emotional moments
- Well-paced revelation of personal information

3. **Visual Storytelling**
- Strong use of family photographs
- Integration of historical footage
- Effective use of typography and graphics

### Areas for Improvement

1. **Structural Balance**
- The 9/11 sequence, while powerful, feels somewhat abrupt in the overall narrative
- The transition between some historical segments could be smoother
- Some temporal jumps might benefit from clearer contextual markers

2. **Technical Elements**
- Some audio transitions between interview segments could be more refined
- The "glitch" effect, while creative, might be overused
- Some archival footage could benefit from additional context or explanation

3. **Narrative Focus**
- The documentary occasionally struggles to balance its multiple storylines
- Some historical context could be more fully developed
- The connection between personal and industry changes could be more explicitly drawn

## Overall Assessment

For a first-time filmmaker, Caleb Mills Stewart demonstrates remarkable skill in handling complex narrative threads and sensitive personal material. The documentary succeeds in transforming what could have been a simple career retrospective into a deeply moving exploration of family, resilience, and transformation.

The personal connection between filmmaker and subject adds depth rather than detracting from objectivity, allowing for intimate moments that might not have been possible with a more detached approach. The decision to end with the letter to his father serves as both an emotional culmination and a thematic resolution of the documentary's various threads.

The technical limitations are minor compared to the documentary's emotional and historical impact. The film effectively captures both the broad sweep of aviation history and the intimate details of one family's journey through that history.

Estimados organizadores del Ibiza CineFest,

Permitidme comenzar con una anécdota personal: vine a España como parte de un programa de intercambio entre la Universidad de las Islas Baleares y la Universidad de Texas, planeado para un solo año. Sin embargo, gracias al trabajo de mi madre como azafata, que me permitió viajar sin pagar los costosos boletos internacionales, pude quedarme tres maravillosos años en estas islas que tanto amo.

Fue en las Islas Baleares donde descubrí mi identidad como artista gay, algo que no siempre fue fácil expresar en un lugar tan conservador como Texas. Vivir en España me permitió conectar con mi verdadera esencia y desarrollar mi visión artística con una libertad que nunca había experimentado antes.

Ya tuve el honor de inscribir un cortometraje en el Ibiza CineFest, aunque en ese momento no pude enviarles una carta porque estaba inmerso en el proceso final de edición. Hoy, con más calma, me encantaría ampliar mi participación en el festival con una nueva inscripción, esta vez presentando "Alas Doradas" como parte de Fem-Cinema.

Esta película no solo cuenta la extraordinaria carrera de mi madre, Robyn Stewart, quien sirvió como azafata durante 53 años, sino que también aborda cómo las mujeres han desafiado las normas de género en un campo históricamente marcado por el sexismo.

Creo que Alas Doradas encaja perfectamente en la sección Fem-Cinema. La historia de mi madre es un testimonio de resiliencia, igualdad y el poder transformador de romper barreras, dejando un legado que inspira a las generaciones futuras.

https://vimeo.com/1033268537

Gracias por su tiempo y por la oportunidad de compartir esta historia en un lugar tan especial para mí como Ibiza.

Con cariño,
